          All India SHRUG Shrid (Villages and Towns) Matched to Corresponding Local Governance Bodies Using LGD Codes
          
            2025
            Harvard Dataverse
            
              Dataset Details
              
                
                  This dataset links SHRUG's village and town identifiers to their corresponding local governance bodies using official LGD codes from the Government of India.
                  Each observation is matched to either a Gram Panchayat or an Urban Local Body, enabling governance-level analysis of census and economic data.
                  The matching achieves 90.41% coverage overall, with over 95% accuracy in most major Indian states. Remaining discrepancies are summarized in the documentation.
                
              
            
          
        

        
          Subdistricts of India by Scheduled Status: An Original Dataset Linked to SHRUG
          
            Development Data Lab, 2024
            Harvard Dataverse
            
              Dataset Details
              
                
                  5969 Indian subdistrict level spatial dataset with information on Fifth and Sixth Scheduled Areas of India.
                  Coded with SHRUG subdistrict spatial indicators for ease of merging with other datasets at the Development Data Lab.

title: Research
text:
Indigenous Representation and Governance
    
      
        
        Land rights, forest governance, indigenous politics, and representation
      
      
        
          Property, Power, and Participation: How Land and Political Rights Transform Forest Governance in Tribal India
          
            Dissertation in Progress
          
        

        
          The Politics of Indigenous-Reserved Seat Vacancies in India's Village Councils
          
            With Alyssa Heinze
            Work in Progress
          
        

        
          Votes without Ideological Conversion: The Case of Hindu Nationalism and Indigenous Voters in India
          
            Under Review
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Religious nationalist parties answer to movements that seek ideological transformation alongside votes. I ask what happens to religious identity when such a party reaches a marginalized electorate through local networks, welfare access, and embedded leaders. I describe this route as leader-mediated expansion and argue that it produces mediated incorporation: the party's religious project travels through politicians who must remain credible to voters whose religious lives are plural. Voters may become more open to the movement's claims, while refusing the hierarchy of identities it seeks to impose. I test the argument in India, where the BJP won an indigenous reserved constituency held by its opposition for six decades, drawing on five months of fieldwork, 120 interviews, and a visual conjoint experiment with 678 indigenous Bhil respondents. I show that religious nationalist parties can win new electorates and broaden tolerance for their language without remaking the identities voters use to define themselves.
              
            
          
        
      
    
  

  
    Democratic Resilience and Parties
    
      
        
        Parties, workers, electoral collaboration, and local democracy
      
      
        
          Formal Positions and the Intra-Party Organizational Hierarchy
          
            With Feyaad Allie and Rahul Verma
            Revise and Resubmit
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Party organizations create formal internal positions to manage work and outreach, and party workers use them to pursue advancement. Yet their consequences for hierarchy remain underexplored. We examine how party workers who hold formal positions differ from those who do not using two original surveys from India. In our first survey of 736 workers in one state, position holders are less supportive of intra-party democracy reforms, including internal primaries and the removal of nomination fees. Interviews suggest that position-holders value party organization control and centralization because their own advancement depended on it. In our national survey of 717 workers across 21 states and 17 parties, position holders report greater ambition, party attachment, and political satisfaction. Women and ethnic minorities are as likely as privileged groups to hold these positions, unlike in candidacy and elected office. Formal positions thus emerge as an underexplored threshold of loyalty and gatekeeping within party hierarchy.
              
            
          
        

        
          Pressured from Above, Constrained from Within: Civil Society-Opposition Party Electoral Linkage
          
            With Feyaad Allie
            Under Review
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Across contexts, civil society organizations (CSOs) and opposition parties collaborate during elections when both confront entrenched incumbent governments. However, shared threats do not produce uniform partnerships on the ground. We argue that while restrictive environments encourage CSO-opposition party linkage, internal constituents constrain its local implementation. CSOs deepen collaboration when candidates align with their social mission, allowing leaders to protect organizational autonomy and reputation with members. Parties deepen collaboration when CSOs offer clear electoral value, making ties defensible to party cadres. We test this argument in India using 62 days of election campaign shadowing and original surveys of 730 CSO representatives and 736 party workers. Two survey experiments show variation in the scope, cohesion, and reciprocity expected by both actors during campaigns. This article unpacks the internal dynamics of CSO-opposition party linkage which constrain their shared response during restrictive environments, and reconceptualizes their relationship as negotiated rather than one-sided partisan brokerage.
              
            
          
        

        
          Decentralizing Democratic Erosion: Local Election Suspensions in the World's Largest Democracy
          
            With Alyssa Heinze
            Under Review
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Democratic erosion is typically understood as unfolding at the national- and state-level. We call attention instead to local-level democratic erosion, a strategy that, we argue, consolidates elite political control while avoiding the public scrutiny that more visible forms of erosion invite. We examine this process through the recent, large-scale suspensions of local elections across India, where millions have gone years without local elected representatives. Drawing on five original surveys totaling over 8,000 respondents and 70 interviews, we substantiate an unawareness-based account of citizens' non-opposition to local-level democratic erosion, highlighting three main findings. First, most citizens are unaware that their own local government is suspended. Second, three preregistered vignette experiments show citizens are not apathetic: they perceive meaningful costs to local democratic erosion. Third, a final preregistered information experiment demonstrates that learning of one's local government's unelected status increases willingness to mobilize for democratic restoration.
              
            
          
        

        
          Who Tolerates Dynastic Politicians? Political Ambition and Candidate Evaluation in India
          
            With Rahul Verma
            Under Review
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Dynastic politicians remain central to electoral politics in many democracies, but we know less about which citizens tolerate them. This research note documents a previously unexamined correlate of tolerance: political ambition. Using a nationally representative survey of 1,988 Indian citizens, we show that respondents who say they would consider politics as a career evaluate dynastic politicians more favorably than otherwise similar respondents. Ambitious citizens are more likely to accept party nominations for politicians' children and to rate dynasts as more capable on nine of ten traits spanning influence, service delivery, and political skills. The associations are robust to demographic controls, state fixed effects, survey weights, and a measure of political engagement. Interviews with citizens and party workers provide suggestive evidence for a gatekeeper interpretation: aspirants often describe dynasts as unfair but unavoidable actors whose favor may matter for their own entry and advancement. The evidence is associational, but the pattern establishes that political ambition is linked to accommodation of dynastic power.
              
            
          
        

        
          When Coalitions Overreach: Voter Limits on Coalition-Based Electoral Mobilization by Interest Organizations
          
            With Feyaad Allie
            Working Paper
            
              Read Abstract
              
                Coalition building is central to classic accounts of social movement success. We ask whether the logic carries into electoral mobilization when interest organizations seek to influence partisan politics under restrictive conditions. We argue that organizations carry coalition repertoires from movement politics into elections because coalition work expands reach beyond direct constituencies, helps coordinate groups with uneven capacities, separates partisan campaigning from organizational work, and builds on organizations' reputations as altruistic actors. However, voters evaluate these efforts through a different logic. They place greater weight on particularistic ties and local embeddedness, and become more skeptical of altruistic intent when outreach is conducted through broad coalition labels. We test this argument in India through interviews, campaign observations, and three survey experiments with organizational representatives and voters. We show that organizations adopt coalition based electoral mobilization, but voters impose an overlooked limit on coalition building by withholding trust from coalition outreach in elections.

title: Pratik Mahajan
text:
Hello! जिंदाबाद!
I am a PhD student in the Department of Political Science at Yale University. My research is in comparative politics and the political economy of development, with a focus on indigenous representation and governance, democratic resilience and parties, and South Asia.
My dissertation examines how granting property and representational rights transforms forests and self-governance among indigenous (Adivasi) communities in India. In parallel, I study how citizens, civil society organizations, and political aspirants are linked to parties and elected institutions, and how these relationships shape political representation and democratic resilience.
I bring several years of observing governance, elections, and claim-making in western India, across Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh, to my research. My work combines field research, interviews, survey experiments, and original datasets on rural governance in India.
